headline: Kanzuru is 感 plus する, with suru voiced to zuru by rendaku.

sources.quote: Compound of 感 + する. The suru changes to zuru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

headline: Sei, “cause, reason, fault”, is probably a shift from shoi.

sources.quote: */sjowi/ → */sjoi/ → /ɕoi/ → /ɕei/ → /sei/ → /seː/
Probably a shift from shoi above.

headline: “To eat” began as the humble “to receive” 食ぶ (tabu), the humble form of 賜ぶ (tabu, “to (deign to) give”).

sources.quote: From earlier Old Japanese form 食(た)ぶ (tabu, “to (humbly) receive or get”, from a superior), a verb with the 下二段(しもにだん) (shimo nidan, “lower bigrade”) conjugation pattern. This was the humble form of 賜(た)ぶ, 給(た)ぶ (tabu, “to (deign to) give”, to an inferior), a verb with the full 四段(よだん) (yodan, “quadrigrade”) conjugation pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Most likely related to 給(たま)う (tamau, “to give”, as a superior gives a thing to, or does something for, an inferior).

Compare the historical development of meaning from “to humbly receive” → “to eat”, with the modern use of the humble verb 頂(いただ)く (itadaku, “to receive”) just before eating, in a sense of “I humbly receive this food.”

headline: Massao is older 真青 (masao) with a doubled consonant for emphasis, first cited in the Nippo Jisho of 1603.

sources.quote: Shift in pronunciation from older 真青 (masao), with gemination as an excrescence to express emphasis. First cited to the Nippo Jisho of 1603.

headline: Kan, “pipe”, is from Middle Chinese 管, and the pipe sense is traced back to the writings of Zhuangzi.

sources.quote: /kwan/ → /kan/
From Middle Chinese 管 (kuɑn^X, “pipe, tube”).
The pipe sense is traced back to the writings of Zhuangzi, already an influential text in Japan in the 700s.

The brush handle sense is traced back to the text of the 詩経 (Shikyō, “Classic of Poetry”), an Old Chinese poetry anthology written from the 11th to 7th centuries BCE and already influencing Japanese writing since the mid-700s.
The wind instrument sense is sourced from the 延喜式 (Engishiki) of 927.

sources.quote: /urutapu/ → /uttafu/ → /uttaheru/ → /uttaeru/
Attested in the historical record since at least the early Heian period.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 訴ふ entry.

headline: Ōu is the Old Japanese verb 覆ふ (opu, “cover from above”) plus ふ (-fu), which expresses repetition or ongoing state.

sources.quote: /opu pu/ → /opopu/ → /ofofu/ → */owou/ → /oːu/
From the Old Japanese verb 覆(お)ふ (opu, “cover from above”) + ふ (-fu, auxiliary verb modifier, expressing repetition or ongoing state).

headline: Tō, “tower”, abbreviates 卒塔婆 (sotoba), a transliteration of Sanskrit stūpa, “heap”.

sources.quote: /tapu/ → /taɸu/ → */tawu/ → /tau/ → /tɔː/ → /toː/
From Middle Chinese 塔 (MC thap, “tower, pagoda, spire”).
An abbreviation for 卒塔婆 (sotoba, sotōba), a transliteration of Sanskrit स्तूप (stūpa, “heap”).

headline: Su, “nest”, is found in the Kojiki of 712, from Proto-Japonic *su.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Found in the Kojiki of 712, and included in the Man'yōshū with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 須 (su). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *su.

headline: Chii is from Middle Chinese 地位, first cited in Japanese in the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 地位 (MC dijH hwijH). First cited in Japanese to a text from the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing from Chinese 地位 (dìwèi).

headline: Sensu is first attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 扇子.
First attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.
